summary: Describes how to use the Generic Routing Encapsulation header for network virtualization in multi-tenant data centers. It decouples virtual networks from the physical network so tenants are isolated. It also introduces a network virtualization framework to illustrate use cases.

plainLanguage.summary: NVGRE carries a tenant's Ethernet traffic inside GRE packets across an IP network. A VSID identifies which virtual network the traffic belongs to, so that traffic can remain separate from other tenants' traffic.

questions: how does gre provide network virtualization in data centers
how does nvgre use gre key field
what is a virtual subnet identifier
subtitle: Using GRE encapsulation to carry isolated virtual networks across an IP network.

tldr.problem: Data centers need to isolate many virtual networks without tying each network to the physical location of its workloads.
tldr.mechanism: NVGRE carries an Ethernet frame inside GRE over IP. A 24-bit Virtual Subnet Identifier (VSID) in the GRE key identifies the virtual Layer 2 network.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes the data plane and deployment considerations for using NVGRE in multi-tenant data centers.

today: RFC 7637 is an Informational document published in September 2015. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Data Centers Use Network Virtualization
sections.content:
Traditional data-center networks often tie a virtual machine's network to its physical location. Moving a workload can require network reconfiguration, and VLANs provide a limited number of virtual subnets for a shared infrastructure.

Network virtualization separates a virtual network and its addresses from the physical network. This allows virtual machines to move while retaining their addresses, and lets multiple virtual networks share the same physical infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Without network virtualization, moving a virtual machine may require changes to the physical network. NVGRE separates the virtual network from that physical layout.

sections.title: NVGRE Endpoints and Virtual Subnets
sections.content:
An NVGRE endpoint is the boundary between the virtual and physical networks. It encapsulates Ethernet frames for transport and decapsulates them at the other endpoint. The endpoint also applies isolation policy for the virtual subnet.

Each virtual Layer 2 network has a 24-bit VSID. The endpoint needs information about where the destination is located and which VSID applies. The RFC assumes that this information is available through management, control-plane distribution, or data-plane learning.
sections.plainLanguage: An NVGRE endpoint wraps frames before they cross the physical network and unwraps them at the other end. It uses the VSID to identify the virtual subnet for each frame.

sections.title: The NVGRE Packet Fields
sections.content:
NVGRE uses the GRE header defined in RFC 2784 and its Key extension from RFC 2890. The outer IP header carries Provider Addresses used by the physical network. The inner Ethernet frame carries the tenant's original frame and Customer Addresses.

The GRE key is 32 bits: 24 bits carry the VSID and 8 bits carry a FlowID. The GRE Key-present bit MUST be set; the checksum-present and sequence-number-present bits MUST be zero. The protocol type is 0x6558, and the inner Ethernet frame MUST NOT contain an IEEE 802.1Q tag.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer packet is used to move the frame across the physical network. Inside the GRE key, the VSID identifies the virtual subnet and the FlowID supplies per-flow entropy.

sections.title: Traffic and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
For unicast traffic, the endpoint sends the GRE packet to the Provider Address of the destination endpoint. The physical network forwards it using ordinary IP connectivity, and the destination endpoint recovers the original Ethernet frame.

Broadcast and multicast traffic can use assigned multicast addresses or N-way unicast, where the sender sends a copy to each endpoint in the virtual subnet. A sender MUST NOT fragment NVGRE packets. The RFC recommends an underlying network MTU that can carry the larger encapsulated frame.
sections.plainLanguage: The physical network forwards the outer IP packet to the destination endpoint. The RFC describes multicast or copied unicast for group traffic and says the sender must not fragment NVGRE packets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Extending a Layer 2 subnet across a data center increases the scope for spoofing attacks. The RFC identifies IPsec or another IP-based mechanism as possible ways to provide authentication or encryption. It also says the policy-distribution control plane should use existing security protocols.

The GRE checksum is not supported by NVGRE. The RFC therefore recommends a network that provides error detection along the packet path, such as Ethernet cyclic redundancy checking or IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: NVGRE extends virtual subnets across the data center, which can increase spoofing risks. Operators can protect traffic and policy distribution with suitable security mechanisms.
